title: The verse passed on
hookLine: Upatissa hears Assaji's verse, understands, and runs to tell Kolita (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)

cards: Kolita sees his friend coming from a distance, and something has already changed. Not a word has been said. It's in Upatissa's face.

The Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells it simply: Kolita sees that his friend looks calm and clear, and asks him straight out whether he has found the deathless, the thing they both left home to look for.

And Upatissa says yes. Earlier on this path we followed Upatissa behind a quiet monk named Assaji and heard the short verse Assaji gave him. Today is the other half of that morning: what Upatissa did with it.

teach.b: Start with where he went. Upatissa had just understood the thing he left home to look for. He could have stayed to question Assaji, or gone straight to find the Buddha.
Instead he went to Kolita, because that was the pact.
The verse was small enough to carry at a run. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease. Next, what he passed on.
Not his own summary. Not a better version. He gave Kolita the same lines he'd heard, and the text says that on hearing them, Kolita understood too.
Then they thought of someone else.
Their old teacher, Sanjaya, still led a crowd of students, so the two went back and invited him to come with them. He refused, and offered instead to share the leadership of his group.
They said no to that and left, and the Vinaya says many of his students went with them. Last, the arrival.

The text says the Buddha saw the two friends coming from far off and told the monks, in paraphrase: these two will be my chief pair of disciples. Upatissa would be called Sariputta, and Kolita, Moggallana.
Here's what the story keeps doing.
Everyone in it who finds something good turns around and hands it on. Assaji to Upatissa. Upatissa to Kolita.
Both of them to their old teacher. The verse travels because nobody sits on it.

how: Assaji's verse is recited in Buddhist communities as a summary of the teaching, and the story of the two friends is told at temples and in Dhamma talks as the beginning of the Buddha's chief pair of disciples.

o: a heaven where the good live without end
freedom from the round of birth and death
living forever in a body that never ages

games.q: who passed what to whom: tap the pairs.

s: Upatissa went straight to the Buddha after hearing the verse
he went first to Kolita, because of their pact.
Kolita needed the verse explained at length
he heard the same lines and understood too.
the two friends invited their old teacher to come with them
Sanjaya refused, but many of his students went along.

games.q: you're Upatissa and Kolita. you've found what you were looking for, and your old teacher Sanjaya still leads a crowd of students. what do you do?
o: slip away quietly and say nothing.
go back and invite him to come with you.
stay and win over his students yourselves.
games.why: they go back and invite him. he refuses and offers them a share in leading his group instead. they leave, and many of his students go with them.

practice: Find one thing from the last week that helped you, a sentence someone said, a song, a recipe that worked, and bring to mind the face of the person who would want it.
Don't polish it or add to it; just hold the two together, the gift and the friend, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Deathless. The thing Upatissa tells Kolita he has found, after hearing Assaji's short verse and understanding it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: 'the things that arise from a cause', the opening words of Assaji's verse.

carryVoice: Your line: he ran to tell him. The same verse, unchanged, from one friend to the next. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 1.23–24 (Sariputta and Moggallana: the verse, the pact kept, Sanjaya, the arrival)
